title: Oat Whisky Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: How oats behave in a whisky mash, why they are hard work, what they add to texture and how oats fit into Irish pot still tradition.
teaser: Oats make porridge thick. They do the same to a whisky mash. Here is why some distillers still use them.
standfirst: Oats are an old whisky grain that almost disappeared. A few distillers are bringing them back for the creamy, oily texture they give. This guide covers how oats behave in the mash tun, the fermenter and the still.
sections:
Oats were a common part of Irish pot still mash bills in the nineteenth century, alongside malted and unmalted barley. They fell out of use as distillers moved to grains that were easier to process and gave more alcohol per tonne. Today the rules for single pot still Irish whiskey allow up to 5% of other cereals such as oats or rye, alongside at least 30% malted and 30% unmalted barley.

Craft distillers in several countries now make whiskies with a much higher oat share, sometimes from malted oats. Where the result can be sold as whisky and under what name depends on each market's rules.

Oats differ from barley in three ways that matter in a distillery. Hulled oats carry a thick husk, often a quarter or more of the grain's weight, so there is less starch per tonne. Oats are rich in beta-glucan, a gum that makes the mash thick and slow to drain. They also contain more fat than most cereals, commonly several percent of the grain.

The result is lower yield and a sticky mash. A distiller used to barley will notice it at once: wort runs off slowly, pumps work harder and the spent grain is heavier.

The husk is the one advantage. Hulled oats form a loose filter bed, which can help lautering when they are mixed with malted barley. Rolled or dehulled oats give no such help and behave more like flour.

Beta-glucanase enzymes break down the gums. Many distillers add them early in the mash or use a rest in the 40s °C before raising to the saccharification temperature in the low to mid 60s °C. Malted oats bring some enzymes of their own, though less than barley malt. A high oat mash usually needs malted barley or added enzymes to convert fully. Our guide to mashing for malt whisky covers the barley baseline.

Oat worts foam more than barley worts because of the beta-glucan and protein. Leave extra headspace in the washback and use antifoam if needed. In the wash still, charge a little lower than usual for the first runs and heat gently at the start, when foaming is worst.

The fat in oats can carry through into the wash and show as oily notes in the spirit. Some distillers like that. Others manage it with cut points. The feints receiver will tell you if oils are building up: watch for a layer forming on top.
What oats bring to the glass

Oat spirit is often described as creamy, oily and full in the mouth, with a soft cereal or porridge note. The texture is the main attraction. Mixed with malted barley, a modest share of oats can add body to a spirit without changing its main flavour much.

Maturation shapes the result as much as the grain. A refill cask keeps the oat texture visible. A fresh sherry or virgin oak cask can cover it. Our guide to malt, grain and blended whisky places these grain whiskies in context.

Oats can be malted, though they are trickier than barley. The husk is thick and the grain takes up water differently, so maltsters adjust steeping and germination. Malted oats bring a little enzyme power and a toasted, nutty note. Raw oats bring more of the creamy texture but no enzymes at all.

Many distillers working with oats use both: malted barley as the enzyme engine, with raw or malted oats making up a share of the grist. Start with a modest share and increase it only once you know how your mash tun copes. A false bottom that runs freely with barley can clog quickly once oat gums are in the mash.

Expect fewer litres of pure alcohol per tonne from oats than from barley malt, mainly because of the husk and lower starch. Track your yield on every batch and compare it with the supplier's spec. If oat whisky is a premium product, the lower yield can be built into the price. If it is a volume product, oats will hurt your cost per litre.

Oats are grown in India mainly as a fodder crop and for the food market, so distilling grade oats or malted oats may need to be imported. Check moisture and storage carefully in humid months.

Run a pilot mash with 20% oats and 80% malted barley. Record run off time, extract and final gravity. Then try 40% oats with beta-glucanase added. Comparing the two will show you how far you can push oats on your own kit before the mash tun slows to a crawl.
faqs: Can whisky be made from oats?
Yes, oats are a cereal and can be used in whisky. Single pot still Irish whiskey allows up to 5% other cereals such as oats, while some craft distillers make whiskies with much more.
Why are oats difficult to distil?
Oats have a thick husk, lots of beta-glucan and more fat than most cereals. They give lower yield, sticky mashes and more foam.
What do oats add to whisky?
Oats are often credited with a creamy, oily texture and a soft cereal note.
Usually yes. Beta-glucanase thins the mash. Malted barley or added enzymes help convert the starch fully.
